newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma says may extend parliament's term.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma says may extend parliament's term.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma said on Friday he might extend parliament's term, due to expire in March 1998, by one year despite protests from some deputies that the move would violate Ukraine's constitution.
"I am ready to consider the question of extending parliament's duties by one year," Kuchma said in a speech at celebrations on the eve of the first anniversary of Ukraine's post-Soviet constitution.

Kuchma, speaking at the Kiev opera house about two hours after the conservative-dominated parliament approved this year's budget six months into the year, said parliament should "consider economic reforms" in this extended period.
"This period must be used to approve laws in the economic sphere," he said, making clear that he wanted deputies to have more time to approve reforms which they have resisted.
Some deputies said the move would violate the constitution, which says parliament is elected for a four-year term.
While the president can call early elections if he disbands the chamber, the constitution says nothing about extending its term.
"Probably Kuchma is afraid the next parliament will be even more conservative," said Ivan Zayats, a leading national democratic deputy.
"But the president and government must at least do something to improve the economic situation. If they can't succeed in half a year, they won't succeed in a year and a half," he said.

Kuchma, author of Ukraine's first economic reform programme in 1994, said he had no plans to postpone presidential elections due in October 1999. But regional administrative leaders elected in parallel with this parliament might have their terms extended, he said.

Kuchma criticised parliament for this year's budget delay and slowness in implementing economic reforms, and said deputies would take the summer off and then begin campaigning instead of working on the economy.
He also said parliament must adopt the 1998 budget by the end of this year.

Parliament has been reluctant to accept reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, which said on Friday it might issue Ukraine with another stand-by loan instead of a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility intended for countries undertaking painful structural reforms.
